newsitem.title: USA: Rich nations to back expanded debt relief for poor.
newsitem.headline: Rich nations to back expanded debt relief for poor.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
Rich industrial countries were poised on Saturday to sharply increase the amount of help they are prepared to offer debt-ridden poor nations under a multibillion-dollar international initiative.

A senior Canadian official said he expected the Group of Seven (G7) to endorse an expansion of the debt relief they and other creditor countries were willing to provide. Under the new plan, 80 percent of poor nations' debts would be forgiven, compared with 67 percent now.
"It looks as though we should be able to secure that today," the official, who declined to be named, told reporters ahead of Saturday's meeting of the G7.
That should pave the way for the formal launch of the multilateral debt relief plan during the current annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank that winds up on October 3.

Saturday's gathering of finance ministers and central bankers from the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- was taking place on the fringes of the annual meeting. It was scheduled to start over lunch and finish after 5:00 p.m. (2100 GMT).

Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin separately told reporters that he was "optimistic" that an agreement could be reached among creditor countries to provide up to 80 percent debt relief to poor nations. But he declined to say whether that would come at Saturday's G7 meeting.

The three-pronged debt-relief initiative -- involving actions by the Paris Club of creditor countries, the IMF and the World Bank -- is aimed at putting debt-ridden poor nations, many of them in Africa, back on their feet.
Uganda is expected to be the first country to benefit from the plan.

Both the World Bank and the IMF had urged the Paris Club of creditor nations to expand their debt relief to cover up to 90 percent of their loans to eligible poor nations. But the G7, which forms the backbone of the Club, baulked.

According to some estimates, about four or five countries would not be able to put their economies back on even keel and achieve so-called debt sustainability if the Paris Club only extends 80 percent debt relief.

The Canadian official said that the IMF and World Bank would need to make up the difference to ensure that did not happen. "The balance of resources will need to be made up by the two institutions," he said.
That balance at issue amounts to some $1.2 billion.
The World Bank has already pledged $2 billion to the initiative. It should not have all that much trouble in kicking in some more from the profits it makes on its loans to developing countries.
But the IMF is another matter. As a monetary institution, it does not make profits on its loans.
The IMF board last week pledged to come up with the necessary financing to take part in the debt relief plan, but left open the question of where the money would come from.

The Canadian official said that the IMF would eventually have to sell some of its nearly 104 million ounces of gold to finance its participation in the programme. But he said that a decision on that controversial proposal may not have to be made until 1998 or beyond.

The majority of the G7 back IMF gold sales. But Italy, and especially Germany, are opposed and instead want the IMF to rely on bilateral contributions from its member nations to finance stepped-up aid to poor countries.
